prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks

statement.case_for: I ranked the Higgs observation (B039) first because it is a concrete discovery in nature, but having read the opening ballots I move to the optical lattice clock (B012) as the preferred prize. Three members place it first, six place it in their top three, and the reasons given are independent of one another: a clear mechanism (the magic-wavelength lattice that cancels the light shift), a decisive demonstration, performance near 1e-18 reproduced by several laboratories, and open consequences for tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a redefinition of the second. Most importantly for how the committee works, it is a case where the invention can be tied to named people: Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking the clocks to the accuracy frontier. As a theorist I find that a measurement result of this kind is exactly what 'finding clues in nature' needs, and a two-person credit leaves room under the three-person limit. Opening support is not merit, but here the support rests on substantive and mutually consistent arguments rather than on shared taste.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that optical clocks are an instrument-and-precision achievement, and its largest payoff, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened; the discovery content is less dramatic than the Higgs or a new class of quantum matter. Lindroth says openly that she relies on memory for early priority history, and other lattice-clock groups (NIST, PTB, SYRTE, and ion-clock lines) contributed to the maturation, so the boundary of the two-name credit is clean on paper but not verified from the supplied record. Meanwhile B039 remains, in my view, the most consequential experimental result on the shortlist, and the fact that it splits the committee mainly over attribution should not be mistaken for a weaker scientific case.

responses.point: Kroll argues that B012 has a cleanly bounded credit, since Hall and Hansch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already covered combs and ion clocks, and that the confirmation across Sr, Yb and Hg is strong and the recognition timely.
responses.response: I agree on the maturity and on the two-name fit, and this is what moved me from my first-place ballot. I would qualify the claim of a cleanly bounded credit: that the earlier prizes cover combs and ion clocks does not establish that the neutral-atom lattice contribution has no other claimants, and the supplied record cannot settle priority. I accept the configuration as the best-defined on the shortlist, not as free of doubt.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B029 (IceCube) first and B039 second, stressing that Higgs credit is hard because of two collaborations of thousands, that Della Negra is as much a founder of CMS as Virdee, and that the rules cap the number of laureates.
responses.response: I share the Higgs-credit concern and listed the same difficulty, including Della Negra versus Virdee and Jenni versus Gianotti. I disagree that it should lower the case for B039 itself; the discovery is overdue. But I do not think leadership roles are a reliable proxy for decisive scientific authorship, and I cannot defend any three-name selection from the record in front of us, which is why I now favour B012 first and keep B039 as the principal alternative, to be revisited if the committee can agree a defensible choice of names.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B051) first but notes that the 2025 prize already recognised superconducting circuits, and ranks B012 second with a clean two-person credit and timely redefinition of the second.
responses.response: Her caution about the 2025 prize is well taken and is one reason I do not push B051; it makes me wary of returning to the same area so soon. Her view that B012 is clean and timely supports my move. I would add that her reliance on field familiarity for B051 is a strength of her assessment, but it does not by itself separate B051 from other quantum-technology candidates.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B012 first and B057 (topological insulators) second, noting that the B057 trio is a plausible theory-plus-experiment set but that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D materials work lie outside the credited names.
responses.response: I ranked B057 second and agree with that diagnosis: the concept is deep but the credited trio is structurally fragile, and I made the same point about Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. This is why I put B057 behind B012 in the preferred configuration. I would not rule it out; a conceptual advance of this scope may eventually need a configuration that the supplied names do not offer.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B005 (MgO tunnelling) first as a case where first-principles theory predicted the effect and experiment delivered it, but concedes that novelty relative to the 2007 GMR prize must be argued.
responses.response: I find the theory-prediction-then-experiment structure attractive, but I disagree that it should lead the list. The GMR neighbour is a real weakness, and a prize that reads as an extension of 2007 would be harder to justify than one that opens a new measurement frontier. The concept is also more a device-engineering story than a new insight into nature.

uncertainties: Whether the early priority history of the magic-wavelength lattice clock supports exactly Katori and Ye, since several members rely on memory for this.
Whether a defensible three-person set exists for B039 given Della Negra, Jenni, Gianotti and Virdee, and whether leadership role can stand in for scientific authorship.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as a precondition for recognising B012 or simply as a confirmation of its impact.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My documented ties (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not connect to any shortlisted candidate or credited name that I can identify, and I do not claim any connection beyond that.
